html:
The Royal Botanical Expedition to New Granada was a scientific survey of the plants of what is now Colombia, led by the Spanish doctor and priest José Celestino Mutis from 1783 until 1816.

Based in Bogotá, it employed painters who made thousands of detailed plant illustrations, and studied quinine bark, the cinchona used against malaria. Mutis trained young creoles in science, among them the geographer Francisco José de Caldas. Alexander von Humboldt visited in 1801.

Many of its members joined the movement for independence, and Caldas was shot by the Spanish in 1816, when the expedition's papers and drawings were shipped to Madrid. They are still in the botanical garden there. The expedition was a seed of science and of national feeling in Colombia.
